summary: This paper evaluates error mitigation and finite-shot sampling on an IBM Quantum Heron processor using a fixed measurement budget, finding that standard zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) and pilot-variance-based adaptive shot allocation do not uniformly improve mean-squared error relative to uniform allocation or raw measurement. Hardware experiments on 156-qubit ibm_marrakesh with median two-qubit error $2.99 \times 10^{-3}$ and readout error $1.45 \times 10^{-2}$ show that adaptive ZNE outperformed uniform allocation at only 2 of 6 tested budgets (average MSE ratio 2.16), and that coupler selection from calibration data produced errors comparable to multiple circuit layers.
motivation: Quantum error mitigation trades bias reduction for increased variance, but nearly all prior benchmarks report accuracy improvements without accounting for the sampling cost incurred under fixed measurement budgets, making it unclear whether mitigation actually reduces mean-squared error in practice.
method: A bias-variance-aware framework decomposing mean-squared error into bias and variance components was applied on physical hardware using Qiskit Runtime V2 primitives, comparing raw measurement, readout mitigation, uniform-allocation ZNE, adaptive shot-budgeted ZNE (ASB-ZNE) using Neyman-optimal allocation seeded by a 100-shot pilot, and dynamical decoupling ($XY_4$ sequences) across GHZ states, repeated-layer circuits ($L \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$), and QAOA MaxCut.
result: On ibm_marrakesh, readout mitigation provided negligible benefit; dynamical decoupling improved estimates only at shallow depth ($L=1,2$) and not where two-qubit gate error dominated; ZNE increased bias for parity observables (bias $1.70 \times 10^{-2}$ vs. raw $5.07 \times 10^{-3}$) while succeeding for QAOA energy; adaptive shot allocation was worse than uniform at 4 of 6 budgets ($B \in \{900, 3000, 12000, 21000\}$ shots) with mean ratio 2.16; and qubit-coupler placement effects ($\langle ZZ \rangle$ dropping from 0.909 to 0.751 between low and high-error couplers) matched or exceeded depth-induced decay.
